clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic MVK variants reducing mevalonate kinase activity; partial deficiency produces the hyper-IgD phenotype while near-complete deficiency causes severe mevalonic aciduria with dysmorphism, cataracts, ataxia and developmental delay.
Onset is typically in the first year of life, and attacks are frequently precipitated by childhood immunisations, minor infections, physical or emotional stress.
The febrile attacks characteristically feature tender cervical lymphadenopathy, prominent abdominal pain with vomiting and diarrhoea, hepatosplenomegaly and arthralgia or arthritis.
Painful oral and genital aphthous ulceration together with a polymorphous rash are common mucocutaneous features.
Serum immunoglobulin D is often elevated but is neither sensitive nor specific and is frequently normal in young children, so a normal level never excludes the diagnosis.
Elevated urinary mevalonic acid excretion during a febrile attack is a useful and more disease-specific pointer than immunoglobulin D.
Interleukin-1 blockade is the mainstay for frequent or severe disease; on-demand non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and short corticosteroid courses help milder attacks.
Reactive AA amyloidosis is less frequent than in familial Mediterranean fever or TRAPS but can still occur with long-standing uncontrolled inflammation.
reference.pathophysiology: Mevalonate kinase catalyses an early step in the mevalonate (isoprenoid and cholesterol) biosynthetic pathway. Reduced enzyme activity, aggravated by the temperature sensitivity of the mutant protein during febrile episodes, limits production of non-sterol isoprenoids required for post-translational prenylation of small GTPases such as RhoA. Deficient geranylgeranylation impairs RhoA-dependent restraint of the pyrin inflammasome, leading to caspase-1 activation and excess interleukin-1 beta. This links the metabolic defect to the autoinflammatory phenotype and explains why blocking interleukin-1 is effective, whereas the accumulation of upstream mevalonic acid itself is a marker rather than the primary driver of inflammation.
additionalDifferentials: Behcet disease with recurrent orogenital ulceration
additionalInvestigations: MVK gene sequencing for biallelic pathogenic variants
Urinary organic acids for mevalonic acid, ideally sampled during a febrile attack
Serum immunoglobulin D and immunoglobulin A concentrations
Mevalonate kinase enzyme activity assay in leucocytes or fibroblasts
Acute-phase reactants during and between episodes
Urinalysis for proteinuria as amyloidosis surveillance in long-standing disease
redFlags: Coexisting cataracts, developmental regression or ataxia suggesting the severe mevalonic aciduria end of the spectrum
Failure to thrive or growth faltering in an infant with recurrent inflammatory attacks
New proteinuria indicating possible AA amyloidosis
An attack with peritonism severe enough to prompt consideration of a surgical abdomen
reference.prognosis: The hyper-IgD phenotype tends to become less frequent and milder with age, and interleukin-1 blockade markedly improves attack control and quality of life. The severe mevalonic aciduria end of the spectrum carries substantial neurodevelopmental morbidity and higher mortality.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because serum immunoglobulin D is normal, particularly in a child under three years of age
Failing to sample urinary mevalonic acid during rather than between attacks
Overlooking vaccination as a characteristic trigger and mislabelling post-immunisation attacks as adverse reactions
Not recognising the continuum with mevalonic aciduria when neurological or ocular features are present
references: Textbook of Pediatric Rheumatology, Cassidy (current edition)
Eurofever and PRINTO consensus classification criteria for hereditary recurrent fevers
